questions.stem: A 26 year old woman has taken ibuprofen 400 mg three times a day for 3 weeks for period pain. She now has epigastric burning and nausea. An OGD shows diffusely red, inflamed gastric mucosa with a few superficial erosions. There is no break through the mucosa and the duodenum is normal. Biopsies are negative for H. pylori.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Gastritis is inflammation of the gastric mucosa without ulceration; NSAIDs damage the protective mucosal barrier, and without a mucosal break this is not an ulcer.

steps.x: It asks for a diagnosis-type answer: build the picture from the history, observations and tests.

clues: ibuprofen 400 mg three times a day
steps.x: NSAID use, inflamed gastric mucosa, but no ulcer.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: NSAID-induced gastritis.

elim: The duodenum is normal at endoscopy.
Needs a normal endoscopy; hers shows inflammation.
An ulcer is a break through the mucosa, and there is none.
Gives heartburn and oesophagitis, not inflamed gastric mucosa.

steps.x: **D. Gastritis.** Gastritis = gastric inflammation without ulceration; NSAIDs and H. pylori are the two main causes.

questions.stem: A 34 year old man has had gnawing epigastric pain for 6 weeks. It comes on about 3 hours after meals and wakes him in the early morning. Eating biscuits or drinking milk eases it. He takes no medicines. There is mild epigastric tenderness. His pulse rate is 72 bpm and BP 126/80 mmHg. A stool H. pylori antigen test is positive.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Duodenal ulcer pain is relieved by eating or milk and is worse before food or at night; about 90% are caused by H. pylori.

steps.x: It asks for a diagnosis-type answer: build the picture from the history, observations and tests.

clues: wakes him in the early morning
Eating biscuits or drinking milk eases it
H. pylori antigen test is positive
steps.x: Pain before food and at night, relieved by eating, H. pylori positive.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Duodenal ulcer.

elim: Right upper quadrant pain after fatty meals, not relieved by eating.
Pain radiates to the back with steatorrhoea, usually in heavy drinkers.
Pain is typically worsened, not relieved, by eating.
Retrosternal burning worse lying flat, not hunger pain relieved by food.

steps.x: **C. Duodenal ulcer.** Hunger pain relieved by food + night pain + H. pylori = duodenal ulcer.

questions.stem: A 58 year old man takes aspirin 75 mg daily after a stroke. For 2 months he has had epigastric pain that starts within 30 minutes of eating. He has started skipping meals because of it and has lost 3 kg. There is epigastric tenderness. His haemoglobin is 128 g/L. He has no vomiting or dysphagia.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Gastric ulcer pain is typically worsened by eating and more often comes with weight loss; aspirin is a key cause to seek.

steps.x: It asks for a diagnosis-type answer: build the picture from the history, observations and tests.
Aspirin use, pain worse on eating, food avoidance and weight loss.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Gastric ulcer.

elim: Right upper quadrant pain after fatty meals without weight loss from food avoidance.
Back-radiating pain with steatorrhoea, usually alcohol-related.
Pain is relieved by eating, not brought on by it.
Retrosternal burning, not food-provoked epigastric pain with weight loss.

steps.x: **D. Gastric ulcer.** Pain worse with food + weight loss = gastric ulcer; relieved by food = duodenal ulcer.

questions.stem: A 74 year old man takes aspirin and clopidogrel after a coronary stent. He has passed black, sticky, foul-smelling stools for 2 days and feels dizzy on standing. He drinks 6 units of alcohol a week and has no stigmata of liver disease. His pulse rate is 112 bpm and BP 96/60 mmHg. Investigations:
questions.q: Which is the most likely source of the bleeding?
questions.e: Bleeding is the most feared complication of peptic ulcer disease, with melaena, coffee-ground vomiting and hypotension; aspirin is a key drug to seek.

steps.x: It asks for a diagnosis-type answer: build the picture from the history, observations and tests.

clues: pulse rate is 112 bpm and BP 96/60 mmHg
steps.x: Antiplatelets, melaena, shock, raised urea from digested blood.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: A bleeding peptic ulcer.

elim: Gives fresh red rectal bleeding, not melaena with a high urea.
Usually gives chronic anaemia and weight loss rather than acute melaena.
Follows forceful vomiting, which he has not had.
Need portal hypertension; he has no liver disease and drinks little.

steps.x: **A. Bleeding peptic ulcer.** Antiplatelets + melaena + shock = bleeding peptic ulcer, the most feared complication.

questions.stem: A 41 year old woman has taken naproxen for back pain for months. Two hours ago she had sudden, severe epigastric pain, now across her whole abdomen and into her right shoulder. She is lying very still. The abdomen is rigid with guarding. Her temperature is 37.6°C, pulse rate 118 bpm and BP 104/66 mmHg. Erect chest X-ray (see item resources).

visual.title: Erect chest X-ray
visual.caption: Free air under the diaphragm: a perforated viscus.

questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Perforation causes sudden severe pain with peritonism (rigid abdomen, guarding, rebound); an erect chest X-ray showing free air under the diaphragm is key.

steps.x: It asks for a diagnosis-type answer: build the picture from the history, observations and tests.
NSAID use, sudden severe pain, peritonism, free air under the diaphragm.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Perforated peptic ulcer.

elim: Gradual right upper quadrant pain with Murphy's sign, no free air.
Pain radiates to the back, and does not cause free air under the diaphragm.
Pain out of proportion to a soft abdomen in a patient with AF or arteriopathy.
Older man with back pain and a pulsatile mass, not free air.

steps.x: **D. Perforated peptic ulcer.** Sudden severe epigastric pain + rigid abdomen + free air under diaphragm = perforated ulcer.

questions.stem: A 69 year old woman started prednisolone 15 mg daily for polymyalgia rheumatica 2 months ago. She also takes levothyroxine, amlodipine and atorvastatin. She now has epigastric pain and nausea after meals. An OGD shows a gastric ulcer and biopsies are negative for H. pylori. She takes no over-the-counter medicines.
questions.q: Which of her medicines is most likely to have contributed?
questions.e: Corticosteroids such as prednisolone are recognised contributors to peptic ulceration; her other drugs do not damage the mucosa.

steps.x: It asks for a diagnosis-type answer: build the picture from the history, observations and tests.
H. pylori-negative ulcer on a corticosteroid.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Prednisolone.

elim: A calcium channel blocker; causes ankle oedema, not ulcers.
Causes myalgia and raised transaminases, not peptic ulcers.
Thyroid replacement does not damage the gastric mucosa.
She is not taking it, and it does not cause ulcers at normal doses.

steps.x: **E. Prednisolone.** Drugs to seek in PUD: NSAIDs, aspirin, bisphosphonates, steroids, KCl, SSRIs, crack cocaine.

questions.stem: A 72 year old man has an acute flare of gout in his right big toe. He was started on a 7 day course of a drug 10 days ago, alongside his regular bendroflumethiazide. He now has epigastric pain and has vomited once. An OGD shows a gastric ulcer. He does not take aspirin.
questions.q: Which drug is most likely to have caused his ulcer?
questions.e: NSAIDs such as indometacin, often used for acute gout, inhibit COX-1 and cause peptic ulcers; colchicine causes diarrhoea instead.

steps.x: It asks for a diagnosis-type answer: build the picture from the history, observations and tests.
Short course for acute gout, then an ulcer.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: An NSAID: indometacin.

elim: Not started in an acute flare and does not cause ulcers.
Can precipitate gout but does not cause peptic ulcers.
Causes diarrhoea and vomiting, not peptic ulcers.
Does not damage the gastric mucosa at normal doses.

steps.x: **D. Indometacin.** Always seek NSAIDs (indometacin, celecoxib) in a patient with a new ulcer.

questions.stem: A 29 year old man has had recurrent epigastric pain for 3 months. He takes no prescribed or over-the-counter medicines and drinks little alcohol. He says he smokes crack cocaine most weekends. A stool H. pylori antigen test is negative. An OGD shows a duodenal ulcer. His BP is 138/86 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most likely cause of his ulcer?
questions.e: Crack cocaine causes intense vasoconstriction of the mucosa and is a recognised cause of peptic ulcers; his negative test and no medicines exclude the two commonest causes.

steps.x: It asks for a diagnosis-type answer: build the picture from the history, observations and tests.

clues: H. pylori antigen test is negative
takes no prescribed or over-the-counter medicines
steps.x: Ulcer without H. pylori or drugs; uses crack cocaine.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Crack cocaine.

elim: Not a recognised cause of peptic ulcer.
Causes villous atrophy, not a duodenal ulcer.
His stool antigen test is negative.
He takes no medicines.

steps.x: **C. Crack cocaine use.** If H. pylori and NSAIDs are excluded, ask about steroids, SSRIs, KCl and crack cocaine.

questions.stem: A 45 year old man has a duodenal ulcer at OGD. He has never taken NSAIDs or aspirin, does not smoke and drinks 8 units a week. He has no family history of note. He asks what is the most likely reason he developed it, and the result of the biopsy is awaited.
questions.q: Which is the most likely cause of his ulcer?
questions.e: Duodenal ulcers are about 4 times more common than gastric ulcers, and about 90% are caused by H. pylori; gastrinoma is a rare cause.

steps.x: It asks for a diagnosis-type answer: build the picture from the history, observations and tests.
Duodenal ulcer, no NSAIDs.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: H. pylori.

elim: He drinks within safe limits, and alcohol causes gastritis rather than most duodenal ulcers.
Zollinger-Ellison syndrome is rare, with multiple ulcers and diarrhoea.
Not the main cause of duodenal ulcers.
Does not cause peptic ulcers.

steps.x: **C. Helicobacter pylori infection.** About 90% of duodenal ulcers are caused by H. pylori.

questions.stem: A 36 year old woman has a 4 week history of burning upper abdominal pain, bloating and indigestion, worse when she is hungry. She has no weight loss, vomiting or dysphagia. Her temperature is 36.8°C, pulse rate 74 bpm and BP 118/72 mmHg. Her abdomen is soft. She is examined by her GP.
questions.q: Which is the most likely finding on examination?
o: Rebound tenderness in the right iliac fossa
questions.e: Examination in uncomplicated peptic ulcer disease shows epigastric tenderness; the other signs belong to other conditions or complications.

steps.x: It asks for a diagnosis-type answer: build the picture from the history, observations and tests.

clues: burning upper abdominal pain, bloating and indigestion
steps.x: Uncomplicated peptic ulcer symptoms.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Epigastric tenderness.

elim: Suggests gastric cancer, not in a well 36 year old with no alarm features.
A sign of acute cholecystitis.
A sign of appendicitis.
A sign of ascites.

steps.x: **A. Epigastric tenderness.** Uncomplicated PUD: epigastric tenderness with nausea, bloating and indigestion.

questions.stem: A 63 year old man takes naproxen for knee osteoarthritis. This morning he vomited a cupful of dark brown granular material. He feels faint. His pulse rate is 106 bpm and BP 102/64 mmHg. A rectal examination is performed in the emergency department as part of his assessment.
questions.q: Which is the most likely finding on rectal examination?
questions.e: A bleeding peptic ulcer causes coffee-ground vomiting and melaena (digested blood gives black tarry stool) with hypotension; bright red blood suggests a lower source.

steps.x: It asks for a diagnosis-type answer: build the picture from the history, observations and tests.
NSAID, coffee-ground vomiting, tachycardia: upper GI bleed.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Melaena: black tarry stool.

elim: Suggests a lower GI source or a massive brisk upper bleed with shock.
Constipation, unrelated to his presentation.
Seen in irritable bowel or colitis.
Seen in obstructive jaundice.

steps.x: **A. Black tarry stool.** Bleeding ulcer = coffee-ground vomiting + melaena + hypotension.

questions.stem: A 30 year old man has a 2 month history of dyspepsia. He has no weight loss, anaemia, vomiting or dysphagia, and takes no NSAIDs. He has not taken a proton pump inhibitor for a month. Examination shows mild epigastric tenderness only. His GP wants to test for H. pylori.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate investigation?
questions.e: Urea breath test or stool antigen test are preferred over serology, which cannot distinguish current from past infection.

steps.x: It asks for an investigation: think what answers the clinical question right now.

clues: no weight loss, anaemia, vomiting or dysphagia
steps.x: Young, no alarm features, needs a non-invasive H. pylori test.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Stool antigen test (or urea breath test).

elim: A marker of bowel inflammation, not H. pylori.
Stays positive after eradication, so less useful than breath or stool tests.
Not needed in a young patient without alarm features.
Needs endoscopy, not indicated without alarm features.

steps.x: **C. Stool antigen test.** Test for H. pylori with urea breath test or stool antigen, both preferred over serology.

questions.stem: A 42 year old woman has dyspepsia without alarm features. Her GP plans a urea breath test for H. pylori. She has been taking omeprazole 20 mg daily, bought over the counter, for the last 3 weeks and it has helped a little. She is otherwise well and takes no NSAIDs.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate next step before testing?
o: Stop omeprazole for 2 weeks before the test
Stop omeprazole for 24 hours before the test
questions.e: PPIs suppress H. pylori urease activity, so standard UK practice is a 2 week PPI washout before a breath or stool antigen test.

steps.x: It asks for an investigation: think what answers the clinical question right now.
PPI use before an H. pylori breath test.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Stop the PPI for 2 weeks first.

elim: Makes a false negative even more likely.
Too short; a 2 week washout is needed.
PPIs suppress H. pylori and can give a false negative.
Less accurate than breath or stool tests and cannot show active infection.

steps.x: **B. Stop omeprazole for 2 weeks before the test.** Stop PPIs 2 weeks before a urea breath test or stool antigen test to avoid false negatives.

questions.stem: A 50 year old man has a 6 week history of epigastric pain and indigestion. For 2 weeks food has also been sticking when he swallows. He has not lost weight and has no anaemia. He takes no NSAIDs. His pulse rate is 78 bpm and BP 132/82 mmHg. Abdominal examination shows mild epigastric tenderness.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate next step?
o: Stool antigen test and treat if positive
Trial of full-dose PPI for 4 weeks
questions.e: Dysphagia is an alarm symptom, so he needs an urgent 2-week-wait OGD whatever his age; test and treat is only for those without alarm features.

steps.x: It asks for an investigation: think what answers the clinical question right now.

clues: food has also been sticking when he swallows
steps.x: Dyspepsia with dysphagia, an alarm feature.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Urgent 2-week-wait OGD.

elim: Dysphagia is an alarm symptom needing urgent referral.
Delays diagnosis of a possible cancer.
Test and treat is only for patients without alarm symptoms.
Masks symptoms and delays urgent endoscopy.

steps.x: **E. Urgent 2-week-wait OGD.** Alarm symptoms (dysphagia, anaemia, vomiting, or ≥55 with weight loss) = 2-week-wait OGD.

questions.stem: A 61 year old woman has had dyspepsia for 4 months. A stool H. pylori test was negative and 8 weeks of full-dose PPI has not helped. She has no weight loss, anaemia, vomiting or dysphagia. Her haemoglobin is 132 g/L. Examination is normal apart from mild epigastric tenderness.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate next step?
o: Continue PPI and review in 6 months
questions.e: NICE advises non-urgent endoscopy for people over 55 with treatment-resistant dyspepsia not meeting 2WW criteria; 2WW is for weight loss or other alarm features.

steps.x: It asks for an investigation: think what answers the clinical question right now.

clues: 8 weeks of full-dose PPI has not helped
no weight loss, anaemia, vomiting or dysphagia
steps.x: Over 55, treatment-resistant dyspepsia, no alarm features.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Non-urgent OGD.

elim: Less sensitive than endoscopy and cannot take biopsies.
Treatment-resistant dyspepsia over 55 needs endoscopy.
Already negative; repeating will not explain resistant symptoms.
She has no weight loss or other alarm features.

steps.x: **C. Non-urgent OGD referral.** Over 55 + treatment-resistant dyspepsia without 2WW criteria = non-urgent endoscopy (NICE).

questions.stem: A 66 year old man was admitted 4 hours ago with two episodes of coffee-ground vomiting and melaena. He takes diclofenac. After IV fluids and a blood transfusion his pulse rate is 92 bpm and BP 118/74 mmHg. His haemoglobin was 84 g/L. The gastroenterology registrar reviews him on the ward.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate diagnostic investigation?
questions.e: OGD with biopsy is the gold standard: it confirms a bleeding ulcer and allows endoscopic treatment; a breath test cannot.

steps.x: It asks for an investigation: think what answers the clinical question right now.

clues: After IV fluids and a blood transfusion
steps.x: Resuscitated upper GI bleed on an NSAID.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Endoscopy (OGD).

elim: Cannot treat bleeding and is unsafe in acute bleeding.
Tests for H. pylori but does not confirm a bleeding ulcer.
Melaena with coffee-ground vomiting points to an upper GI source.
Not the first test for a suspected bleeding ulcer.

steps.x: **B. Upper GI endoscopy.** OGD is the gold standard for PUD and confirms (and treats) a bleeding ulcer.

questions.stem: A 64 year old woman had an OGD for dyspepsia that showed a 1.5 cm ulcer on the lesser curve of the stomach. Biopsies were benign and positive for H. pylori. She has completed eradication therapy and 8 weeks of full-dose PPI. Her symptoms have settled. She asks whether any more tests are needed.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate next step?
questions.e: Repeat endoscopy at 6 to 8 weeks after PPI or eradication confirms healing; this matters because gastric ulcers are more likely to be malignant than duodenal ulcers.

steps.x: It asks for an investigation: think what answers the clinical question right now.

clues: ulcer on the lesser curve of the stomach
completed eradication therapy and 8 weeks of full-dose PPI
steps.x: A gastric ulcer after treatment.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Repeat OGD at 6 to 8 weeks.

elim: Not needed to check ulcer healing.
Gastric ulcers can be malignant, so healing must be confirmed.
Stays positive after eradication, so useless to check cure.
Does not confirm healing or exclude malignancy.

steps.x: **E. Repeat OGD to confirm healing.** Gastric ulcers need repeat endoscopy at 6 to 8 weeks: they are more likely to be malignant.

questions.stem: A 64 year old woman takes diclofenac for hip osteoarthritis. She has had epigastric pain for 6 weeks. An OGD shows a gastric ulcer; biopsies are benign and negative for H. pylori. She is otherwise well. Her pulse rate is 74 bpm and BP 128/78 mmHg. Her haemoglobin is 124 g/L.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate management?
o: Continue diclofenac and add a PPI for 2 weeks
Omeprazole, amoxicillin and clarithromycin for 7 days
Stop diclofenac and give full-dose PPI for 8 weeks
questions.e: The first step is to stop NSAIDs; H. pylori-negative, endoscopy-confirmed PUD is treated with full-dose PPI monotherapy for 4 to 8 weeks.

steps.x: It asks for management: decide how sick the patient is and what changes the outcome next.
NSAID-related, H. pylori-negative, endoscopy-confirmed ulcer.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Stop the NSAID; full-dose PPI for 4 to 8 weeks.

elim: The trigger must be removed, and 2 weeks is too short.
Eradication is for H. pylori-positive ulcers.
Surgery is not needed for an uncomplicated benign ulcer.
Still an NSAID, so the ulcer will persist.

steps.x: **D. Stop diclofenac and give full-dose PPI for 8 weeks.** First remove the trigger, then H. pylori-negative PUD = full-dose PPI for 4 to 8 weeks.

questions.stem: A 37 year old man has a duodenal ulcer at OGD and a positive rapid urease test. He has no drug allergies, takes no regular medicines and has never had antibiotics for H. pylori. He prefers to avoid clarithromycin because it interacts with a medicine his brother once took. His pulse rate is 70 bpm.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate treatment?
o: PPI, amoxicillin and metronidazole for 7 days
PPI, clarithromycin and metronidazole for 7 days
questions.e: H. pylori-positive ulcers need 7 days of triple therapy (PPI + amoxicillin + clarithromycin or metronidazole); PPI alone allows the infection and ulcer to return.

steps.x: It asks for management: decide how sick the patient is and what changes the outcome next.
H. pylori-positive, not penicillin allergic, avoiding clarithromycin.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Triple therapy: PPI + amoxicillin + metronidazole for 7 days.

elim: Single antibiotics fail; eradication needs a PPI and two antibiotics.
Heals the ulcer but leaves H. pylori, so it recurs.
Too short and only one antibiotic.
The penicillin-allergy regimen; he is not allergic.

steps.x: **D. PPI, amoxicillin and metronidazole for 7 days.** H. pylori-positive = 7 days triple therapy: PPI + amoxicillin + clarithromycin or metronidazole.

questions.stem: A 52 year old woman has H. pylori-positive gastritis confirmed by a urea breath test. When she was given penicillin as a child she developed facial swelling and wheeze needing adrenaline. She has never had eradication therapy before. She takes no other medicines. Her GP wants to treat the infection.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate eradication regimen?
o: PPI, amoxicillin and clarithromycin for 7 days
PPI, amoxicillin and metronidazole for 7 days
PPI, clarithromycin and metronidazole for 7 days
questions.e: With penicillin allergy the triple therapy is PPI + clarithromycin + metronidazole, avoiding amoxicillin.

steps.x: It asks for management: decide how sick the patient is and what changes the outcome next.

clues: facial swelling and wheeze needing adrenaline
steps.x: Penicillin anaphylaxis, first eradication attempt.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: PPI + clarithromycin + metronidazole for 7 days.

elim: A second-line option after failed triple therapy.
Does not eradicate H. pylori.
Contains amoxicillin, dangerous after penicillin anaphylaxis.
Contains amoxicillin, a penicillin.

steps.x: **E. PPI, clarithromycin and metronidazole for 7 days.** Penicillin allergy: swap amoxicillin out, giving PPI + clarithromycin + metronidazole.

questions.stem: A 44 year old man had 7 days of omeprazole, amoxicillin and metronidazole for an H. pylori-positive duodenal ulcer. He took every dose. Six weeks later his symptoms persist and a repeat urea breath test, done after stopping his PPI for 2 weeks, is still positive. He has no drug allergies.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate next treatment?
o: Omeprazole, amoxicillin and clarithromycin for 7 days
Omeprazole, amoxicillin and metronidazole for 7 days
questions.e: If first eradication fails, repeat triple therapy and swap metronidazole for the unused clarithromycin (or vice versa).

steps.x: It asks for management: decide how sick the patient is and what changes the outcome next.
Failed first-line triple therapy containing metronidazole.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Repeat triple therapy, swapping to clarithromycin.

elim: Leaves the infection untreated.
Repeats the regimen that failed, risking metronidazole resistance.
Surgery is not used for failed eradication.
Persistent infection keeps the ulcer active.

steps.x: **B. Omeprazole, amoxicillin and clarithromycin for 7 days.** Failed eradication: repeat triple therapy and swap to the antibiotic not used first time.

questions.stem: A 49 year old woman has an H. pylori-positive duodenal ulcer. She has had two courses of triple therapy, first with clarithromycin and then with metronidazole, both with amoxicillin. Her urea breath test remains positive. She has no allergies and took all her tablets. Her GP seeks advice.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate next treatment?
questions.e: After failed triple therapy, alternatives include bismuth-based quadruple therapy or other antibiotics; repeating a failed regimen invites resistance.

steps.x: It asks for management: decide how sick the patient is and what changes the outcome next.
Two failed triple therapies.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Bismuth-based quadruple therapy.

elim: Suppresses acid but does not eradicate the infection.
Historical surgery, not used for resistant H. pylori.
Repeats a failed regimen with likely resistance.
Persistent infection risks ulcer recurrence and bleeding.

steps.x: **A. Bismuth-based quadruple therapy.** Second-line options: swap antibiotic, or bismuth-based quadruple therapy.

questions.stem: A 70 year old man phones his GP surgery. Since this morning he has vomited blood twice and passed a black, tarry stool. He takes ibuprofen for arthritis. He feels lightheaded when he stands. The duty doctor speaks to him on the phone. He lives with his wife and has a car.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate next step?
o: Book a routine GP appointment next week
Prescribe omeprazole and review in 2 days
Request a stool H. pylori antigen test
Stop ibuprofen and refer for a 2-week-wait OGD
questions.e: A bleeding ulcer with haematemesis or melaena needs urgent hospital admission for resuscitation and endoscopy; outpatient plans are unsafe.

steps.x: It asks for management: decide how sick the patient is and what changes the outcome next.
Haematemesis and melaena on an NSAID, with postural symptoms.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Urgent hospital admission.

elim: An upper GI bleed can be life-threatening.
Delays assessment of a possible bleeding ulcer.
Irrelevant to an acute bleed.
Too slow; he needs admission now.

steps.x: **A. Arrange urgent hospital admission.** Haematemesis or melaena = urgent hospital admission.

questions.stem: A 53 year old man has a perforated duodenal ulcer, with free air under the diaphragm on erect chest X-ray. He has received IV fluids, analgesia, antibiotics and a group and save has been sent. His pulse rate is now 98 bpm and BP 118/76 mmHg. He has generalised peritonism.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate definitive management?
questions.e: A perforated ulcer is stabilised with IV fluids and group and save, then definitive management is laparotomy; endoscopic clipping and embolisation are for bleeding.

steps.x: It asks for management: decide how sick the patient is and what changes the outcome next.

clues: group and save has been sent
steps.x: Resuscitated perforation with peritonitis.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Laparotomy.

elim: Used for bleeding ulcers, not perforations.
Needed later, but does not close a perforation.
For bleeding vessels, not perforations.
Generalised peritonitis needs surgery.

steps.x: **E. Laparotomy and surgical repair.** Perforated ulcer: stabilise with IV fluids and group and save, then laparotomy.

questions.stem: A 40 year old man has a urea breath test. He swallows urea labelled with carbon-13, and 30 minutes later labelled carbon dioxide is detected in his breath. His doctor explains that the same enzyme that makes the test positive also lets the organism survive in the acid of his stomach.
questions.q: Which product of this enzyme protects the organism from acid?
questions.e: H. pylori urease converts urea to ammonia, which neutralises acid locally so the organism can survive; the released CO2 is the basis of the urea breath test.

steps.x: It asks for a mechanism: link the finding in the vignette to the underlying process.
Bacterial urease splits urea into CO2 and ammonia.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Ammonia.

elim: Made by the host mucosa, not the bacterium.
This is what the organism must survive.
A host protease, which does not protect the bacterium.
A host mediator of mucosal defence, not a bacterial product.

steps.x: **A. Ammonia.** Urease turns urea into ammonia (neutralising acid) and CO2 (detected in the breath test).

questions.stem: A 38 year old woman has chronic antral gastritis. Biopsies of the gastric antrum show chronic inflammation with curved rod-shaped organisms on the surface epithelium. A rapid urease test on the biopsy turns pink within an hour. The pathologist describes the organism to the medical students.
questions.q: Which best describes this organism?
questions.e: H. pylori is a Gram-negative, urease-producing bacterium that colonises the gastric antrum and causes chronic inflammation.

steps.x: It asks for a mechanism: link the finding in the vignette to the underlying process.
Curved rods in the antrum, urease positive.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: H. pylori: Gram-negative, urease-producing.

elim: Describes mycobacteria, not this gastric organism.
H. pylori is a curved rod, not a coccus.
Describes Clostridium or Bacillus species.
Describes Candida.

steps.x: **C. Gram-negative urease-producing bacterium.** H. pylori = Gram-negative, urease-producing, colonises the antrum and causes chronic inflammation.

questions.stem: A 71 year old woman takes naproxen for osteoarthritis and develops a gastric ulcer. Her H. pylori test is negative and her acid secretion is normal. A medical student asks how a drug taken for joint pain can damage the stomach lining when it does not increase acid production.
questions.q: Which best explains how the drug causes ulceration?
o: Fewer prostaglandins, so less mucus, bicarbonate and mucosal blood flow

questions.stem: A 33 year old man has a duodenal ulcer and H. pylori infection. Gastric function tests show a high basal and stimulated acid output. A second patient, a 70 year old woman with a gastric ulcer, has normal acid output. A tutor asks the students to explain the difference.
questions.q: Which mechanism best explains the man's duodenal ulcer?
o: Impaired mucosal defence with normal acid
questions.e: Duodenal ulcers typically result from increased acid secretion, whereas gastric ulcers more often reflect impaired mucosal defence.

steps.x: It asks for a mechanism: link the finding in the vignette to the underlying process.

clues: high basal and stimulated acid output
steps.x: Duodenal ulcer with high acid output.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Increased acid secretion.

elim: Damages gastric, not duodenal, mucosa.
The typical mechanism of gastric ulcers.
The opposite of what his tests show.
Linked to atrophic gastritis, not duodenal ulcers.

steps.x: **C. Increased gastric acid secretion.** Duodenal ulcers = too much acid; gastric ulcers = weak mucosal defence.

questions.stem: A 76 year old woman with a gastric ulcer has low-normal acid output. Biopsies show mucosal atrophy and chronic inflammation, and she takes low-dose aspirin. Her duodenum is normal. Her doctor explains that her ulcer has formed in a different way from most duodenal ulcers.
questions.q: Which mechanism best explains her gastric ulcer?
questions.e: Gastric ulcers more often arise from impaired mucosal defence than from excess acid, which is the usual duodenal mechanism.

steps.x: It asks for a mechanism: link the finding in the vignette to the underlying process.
Gastric ulcer with low acid and a weakened mucosa.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Impaired mucosal defence.

elim: Gastrinoma gives very high acid and multiple duodenal ulcers.
The typical mechanism of duodenal ulcers; her acid is low-normal.
Would raise acid output.
Not the mechanism of gastric ulcers.

steps.x: **B. Impaired mucosal defence.** Gastric ulcers usually reflect impaired mucosal defence rather than excess acid.

questions.stem: A 68 year old man has a large ulcer high on the lesser curve of the stomach. He vomits fresh blood and becomes shocked. At endoscopy there is a visible vessel spurting at the base of the ulcer. His previous OGD showed a normal duodenum.
questions.q: Which artery is most likely to be bleeding?
questions.e: Ulcers can erode the left gastric artery (lesser curve) or the gastroduodenal artery (posterior duodenal wall), causing life-threatening haemorrhage.

steps.x: It asks for a mechanism: link the finding in the vignette to the underlying process.
A lesser curve gastric ulcer eroding a vessel.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: The left gastric artery.

elim: The usual source for posterior duodenal ulcers, but his ulcer is on the lesser curve.
Supplies the hindgut, not the stomach.
Supply the fundus near the greater curve.
Runs behind the stomach to the spleen; not the lesser curve vessel.

steps.x: **C. Left gastric artery.** Posterior duodenal ulcer = gastroduodenal artery; lesser curve gastric ulcer = left gastric artery.

questions.stem: A 59 year old man had a perforated duodenal ulcer but delayed coming to hospital for 2 days. At laparotomy there is turbid, foul-smelling fluid throughout the peritoneal cavity. His temperature is 39.1°C and blood cultures grow mixed gut organisms. The surgeon explains how the peritonitis evolved.
questions.q: Which sequence best explains his peritonitis?
o: Bacterial peritonitis followed by chemical peritonitis
Chemical peritonitis followed by bacterial peritonitis
Haematogenous spread of bacteria to the peritoneum
questions.e: Perforation spills gastric contents into the peritoneum, causing a chemical peritonitis first and then a bacterial peritonitis as organisms multiply.

steps.x: It asks for a mechanism: link the finding in the vignette to the underlying process.

clues: delayed coming to hospital for 2 days
steps.x: Perforation with delay and infected fluid.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Chemical peritonitis first, then bacterial.

elim: Wrong order; acid and enzymes act first.
The source is the spilled gut contents.

steps.x: **B. Chemical peritonitis followed by bacterial peritonitis.** Perforation spills acid and contents: chemical peritonitis, then bacterial peritonitis.
